slides.label: Title
slides.narration: Open the lecture by framing the chapter question: what can be built with only two tools, a straightedge and a compass? This chapter takes the historically first approach to geometry and shows that these two instruments already generate a surprisingly rich arithmetic. Orient students to printed pages 1 through 19 without quoting the source text directly.

slides.label: Lecture Route
slides.narration: Use this route slide to preview the four main themes. Students should leave able to perform the five basic constructions, explain how constructions encode addition, multiplication, and square roots, apply similar triangles to transfer ratios, and appreciate why the constructible numbers form a proper subfield of the reals.

slides.label: Equilateral Triangle
slides.narration: Walk through the equilateral triangle construction step by step. Emphasize that the two circles of equal radius guarantee the third vertex lies at the correct distance from both endpoints. This is the simplest demonstration that compass arcs can produce exact geometric objects, not approximations.

slides.label: Five Primitives
slides.narration: Present the five foundational constructions as a toolkit. Each one builds on straightedge lines and compass circles, and together they let the geometer bisect segments and angles, drop perpendiculars, and transfer distances. Point out that every later construction in the chapter reduces to sequences of these five primitives.

slides.label: Constructible Arithmetic
slides.narration: Show how straightedge-and-compass steps translate into field operations. Adding and subtracting are segment concatenation, multiplication uses similar triangles with a unit segment, and division inverts the same triangle configuration. The key insight is that geometry encodes algebra without numbers.

slides.label: Similar Triangles
slides.narration: Explain the similar-triangles engine that drives constructible multiplication and division. When two triangles share an angle and their sides are proportional, the ratio transfers lengths from one scale to another. This is the mechanism that lets compass-and-straightedge reach any rational number starting from a unit.

slides.label: Square Root Construction
slides.narration: Demonstrate how the geometric mean construction produces square roots. Given segments of length 1 and a, the semicircle method yields a segment of length square root of a. This extends the constructible field beyond the rationals and explains why certain classical problems like doubling the cube resist solution.

slides.label: Irrationality of sqrt(2)
slides.narration: Present the irrationality of the square root of 2 as the chapter capstone. The proof by contradiction assumes a reduced fraction and derives that both numerator and denominator must be even, violating the assumption. Connect this back to the constructible numbers: sqrt(2) is constructible but not rational, so the compass reaches beyond fractions.

slides.label: Constructible Field
slides.narration: Introduce the constructible number field formally. Starting from the rationals, each compass-and-straightedge step can adjoin at most one square root, so the constructible reals form a tower of quadratic extensions. This algebraic characterization explains why trisecting a general angle and squaring the circle are impossible.

slides.label: Recap
slides.narration: Close the lecture by connecting the five primitives, constructible arithmetic, and the algebraic characterization into a single pipeline. The chapter shows that geometry is not just drawing; it is a computational system whose power and limitations can be precisely described by field theory.
